newsitem.title: FRANCE: BA plan for Air Liberte seen as best offer.
newsitem.headline: BA plan for Air Liberte seen as best offer.

text.p: A plan by British Airways and France's Banque Rivaud to rescue Air Liberte looks like the best offer now available, a court-appointed administrator handling the case of the insolvent French airline said on Tuesday.
"Effectively the establishments making this proposal are serious establishments," Gilles Baronnie told Reuters. "In the current state of affairs, their plan looks like the most probable choice."
He said he expected the Creteil commercial court to rule on Wednesday not to liquidate Air Liberte but to approve its continuation, given that a solid rescue plan had been presented.
Another plan or buyout bid could be put forward before a final decision expected in around six weeks after discussions with Air Liberte's creditors, he said.
Baronnie said he had not seen an offer from Virgin Express, which said earlier that it was planning to outbid BA for Air Liberte, which went into receivership on September 26.
Industry sources said Virgin was in talks with state-owned Air France, but Air France declined any comment.

Air France and French officials were reported to favour a rival bid by Jacques Maillot, chairman of the Nouvelles Frontieres travel company, to establish a domestic rival to Air France's regional carrier Air France Europe.
But Maillot withdrew his proposal last week after failing to strike a financial agreement with his then-partner Banque Rivaud, Air Liberte's biggest shareholder.
Banque Rivaud turned last week to British Airways, which agreed to revise its initial buyout offer to present a joint rescue plan with a French partner to the Creteil court.
"French commercial courts have a tendency to favour continuation plans, which allow for the repayment of creditors," Baronnie said.
But he said a rival buyout proposal would have a chance if it were "interesting" in terms of either job preservation or price or repayment to creditors.
Baronnie said AOM board member and pilot Fernand Danan had proposed a buyout to the Creteil court "but we haven't heard back from him on the financial guarantees."

BA and Banque Rivaud said last week that their plan entailed the preservation of 1,250 of the 1,400 jobs at Air Liberte and investment of 630 million francs in its equity -- 440 million from BA, which would have 70 percent, and 190 million from Banque Rivaud, which would have 30 percent.
They agreed to pay the cost of running Air Liberte during receivership -- estimated at 150 million francs -- and Rivaud would write off convertible debt of just over 500 milion francs.
The two companies plan to offer creditors, owed around 800 million francs, either 20 percent in cash immediately or full payment stretched over 10 years.

Air Liberte lost 650 million francs in the first nine months of 1996. It was hurt by a price war and rapid expansion during the liberalisation of the domestic market ahead of the full opening of the European market in 1997.
British Airways already owns the French TAT airline. TAT and Air Liberte would have a combined 20 percent market share.
